The Department of Psychology requests that the departmental and administrative home of the NVP course code and the interdisciplinary Minor in Nonviolence and Peace Studies be transferred to the Department of Political Science in the College of Arts & Sciences. The NVP course code is a core component for the Global Peace Studies concentration in the Masters in International Relations Program housed in the Department of Political Science. The Department of Political Science will retain all of the existing NVP courses currently in the course catalog. Administration and advising responsibilities for the interdisciplinary Minor in Nonviolence and Peace Studies will be assumed by the Department of Political Science. 6. If applicable, please include the existing URI catalog language and proposed catalog changes indicated in Track Changes.
In addition to fulfilling all the basic requirements for a minor (see Minor Fields of Study), students who declare a minor in nonviolence and peace studies should complete a minimum

of 18 credits, as follows: 1) NVP 200, a one-credit colloquium course on Nonviolence and Peace Studies; 2) a nonviolence training experience such as one of the two-day workshops offered by URI’s Center for Nonviolence and Peace Studies (or training offered by the American Friends Service Committee, Fellowship of Reconciliation, or similar organization), combined with three credits of directed reading/independent study focused on the history, theory, and application of nonviolence. Credits may be earned in HDF 498, HIS 391, HPR 401 or 402, PHL 499, PSC 455 or 456, PSY 489, SOC 498 or 499, and should be chosen in consultation with the student’s advisor for the minor and other faculty; 3) a minimum of one of the following three-credit courses in individual/interpersonal peace processes: COM 221, 422; HDF 450; HPR 107, 110; PSY 479Y, 479H; or SOC 408; 4) a minimum of one of the following three-credit courses in societal/global peace processes: AAF/PSC 380; COM 310, 361; ECN 386; HPR 411; PHL 217; SOC 318; and 5) additional related courses totaling a minimum of 18 credits for the minor, such as AAF/SOC 240, 336; AAF/HIS 359, 366; AAF/SOC 428; COM 310, 322, 421, 461; ECN 381; GWS (WMS) 150, 310, 350, and 351; HDF 230; HIS 328, 349; PSY 103, 334, 335; PSY/SOC 430; SOC 216, 230, 274, 330, 331, 370, 413, 420, 452. Students are responsible for meeting applicable prerequisites for courses in the minor, or for obtaining the instructor’s permission to take a course. Interested students should contact Professor Paul Bueno de MesquitaKristin Johnson in the Department of Psychology Political Science (401.874.54944216 or pauldem@uri.edukristin_johnson@uri.edu). 7. Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages). Health Sciences is a rapidly changing and evolving discipline, requiring highly trained, critical thinkers to solve some of society’s biggest health-related problems. The Ph.D. in Health Sciences is a college-wide degree with faculty from multiple departments/programs in the College of Health Sciences and focuses on health, wellness, and quality of life across the lifespan. Research brings together faculty and students to solve important health-related problems through a mix of basic, applied and translational science. The program allows students the opportunity to gain experience in the various disciplines that make up health sciences and provides them with the opportunity for advanced content knowledge and in- depth training in one discipline or area of study.

Students are eligible to apply for this program after earning a post-baccalaureate degree in a health-related field. Physical Therapy was not initially included as a specialization because the graduate catalog language (which has now been changed) required a master’s degree to have 30 credits from their post-baccalaureate degree apply to their doctoral program. Physical Therapy does not offer a master's degree. Instead, students in this discipline go on to the

doctoral of physical therapy (DPT).
Therefore, no credits from the DPT would count toward the PhD.
The graduate council approved language (Nov. 9, 2020) in the graduate manual to let students with a master’s or qualifying graduate degree request up to 30 credits from this degree to be applied to their doctoral program.
This includes the Doctor of Physical Therapy (DPT) degree.
Given this change, we would like to add Physical Therapy as a specialization to the CHS doctoral program.

Priority Items (40 minutes) 3.1 New ‘home’ for the Interdisciplinary Neuroscience Graduate Programs - The three INP graduate programs (MS, PhD and Certificate) were administratively re-homed from the Graduate School to CHS as a result of the December senate meeting.
Senate officers have heard inquiries and concerns about that move and it appears that a process improvement should be implemented that might ensure program directors are not left out of these decisions.

There were questions about the origins of such proposals and why the system is built in such a way that deans can leapfrog relevant faculty.
Beyond the mechanics of Kuali proposals, there seems to be a need to develop a better model for how interdisciplinary programs are housed at the university.
Pres.
Williams will try to learn more about the genesis of this particular change and the approval process it was subjected to.
FSEC may circle back with tangible suggestions for process improvements but in the meantime, staff was asked to pay particular attention to “administrative” requests in Kuali and alert the FSEC or senate officers to any concerns.
Sen.
Trimm will communicate with CASC about how to approach such proposals, if necessary, and VP Preisser will do the same with the Graduate Council. 3.2 Future Legislation Updates i.
Establishing College Liaisons - The FSEC Officers are meeting with the Council of Deans next week (2/4) and hope to gather their input and use it to refine the draft. ii.
College By-Laws - This remains a secondary priority behind the Liaisons.
FSEC members agree that once the liaison roles are established and liaisons start meeting together, 1

shared information about the disparate operations of the colleges will help make a case for a By-laws mandate or other common governance structure requirements. iii.
Chapter 8 amendments related to 7 & 14 week calendar alignment - VP Preisser provided a synopsis of the plan to roll out a four program pilot of concurrent enrollment options in Fall, 2027.
The affected colleges will need to vote in favor of the plan in order for it to go forward.
The pilot will be subject to review and renewal at the end of four years.
If the Senate elects to reject renewal, the concurrent enrollments will end at the conclusion of the spring, 2031 term.
If the senate determines that the system is working well, the initiative could be expanded.
Questions were asked about the basis for renewal and if expectations can and will be set for a meaningful evaluation.
There was also a concern about institutional memory given that senators sitting at roll-out will cycle off the senate prior to the renewal phase.
VP Preisser noted that it will be up to the programs themselves to initiate their renewal so the senate will not need to ‘remember’ to do it.

A final draft is expected today and FSEC agreed to forward it to TAAC, CBUM and the ACC for review.
The legislation will be introduced in February and docketed for action in March, if ready. iv.
Clarifying and specifying launch date for SGO and 4+ attempt legislation - Staff is preparing amendments to FSEC Bills 4 and 5 to include the effective dates (Fall 2026) and will ensure that future bills all include an effective date. v.
Approval of academic calendars 8 years in advance - The Graduate School has expressed a need to set the calendar eight years in advance and such a change would require amending Sec. 8.70.10 of the UM, which prescribes a 6-year calendar.
This move would temporarily add to the workload of the ACC, which would be tasked with preparing and presenting for approval two additional calendars all in one year.
The Committee is responsible for setting the Summer, Online, standard academic year calendars, including J-term, but would need to close the gap between the 6- and 8- years out versions.
The amendment itself is straightforward and could be introduced in February. vi.

Adjusting due date for final grades - There are concerns about the timelines associated with faculty entering final grades after exams, academic standing notifications being generated, and students having adequate time to react to those notifications, especially if they need to file a grade appeal or are facing a negative finding regarding their academic standing.
URI faculty often benefit from ample time to report grades, but sometimes face quicker turnarounds.
The administration recently suggested running an AI model to determine a standard that might be optimal for students,faculty, and advising staff.
FSEC members suggested that no such effort is likely necessary, because a quick look at the due dates for the last four years reveals that faculty have not faced a deadline earlier than six days post-exam.
It would be simple and probably agreeable to simply establish that time frame as a standard.
There was some concern about the fall semester in particular, since the deadline could bump up against the Christmas holiday.
Pres.

Williams revealed that Fannon Institute Director Kim Stack has done some research on this matter and found that at most peer institutions, the norm for grade posting is 72 hours after the exam is completed.
It will be important to emphasize that the time of the staff involved in generating the standing reports is valuable too, and a balance needs to be struck between faculty preferences and the needs of staff to generate adequate and timely reports that serve students’ needs. 2

Williams reached out to the departments involved in the Program to gain feedback on the re-homing to the College of Education from the Graduate School.
There seemed to be some misunderstanding of how the budget model works.

It requires that the “money follows the instructor” which means that the departments will keep revenue for their courses and those funds will not be diverted to the CoEdu.
But there does seem to be opacity around the administrative apparatus.
The college is simply responsible for ‘stacking’ the certificates that the departments offer, and will likely get to count the graduates in their degree conferral numbers.

Van Wyk consented to launch and manage this service for the foreseeable future.
Pres.
Williams noted he needs to present the idea to the Provost’s office for a reaction before the initiative goes to the senate, possibly for a March introduction.
The senate office is happy to host the resource and forms on their webpage with links to the Provost’s pages, if desired. iv.
Senate appointments to Library Dean search - Pres.
Williams has completed the appointment of two faculty members. v.
Copyright statement - No report ; still under review by the General Counsel. vi.
Commencement schedule - FSEC assignments - TBD following election of a new VP/President-elect (on 2/29), who should be given the opportunity to choose the extent of their role. vii.
Chapter 2 UM amendments - Status of revisions - for February adoption?
There were some related concerns about the decision to split the position of the Vice Provost for Academic Personnel and Budget in two.

Some edits to the draft are in progress and it is hoped that the senate is still on track to accept the changes in February. 6.
Report of the Coordinator i.
Student worker hiring update - The FS office is on-boarding two graduate student workers who are starting right away. ii.
Senate elections and February VP election - Staff is waiting for the current full-time faculty list from the Provost’s team which is required to prepare apportionment notices.
The office is also designing an electronic ballot for the VP election, which will run differently this year than in years past due to new UM updates. iii.
Parliamentarian - The FS Parliamentarian serves at the pleasure of the FS President and this individual does not need to be a senator to serve.
If the current Parliamentarian continues past his term expiration, FSEC should consider providing compensation.
FSEC members agreed unanimously. iv.
New question - What prevents a faculty member from teaching in another department?
This question was raised to staff from a sitting senator who offered the example of an Engineering faculty member being qualified to teach calculus or physics from inside the engineering department.

FSEC members explained that course codes belong to department heads;additionally, per the AAUP contract, chairs are responsible for assigning teaching responsibilities. 7.
New Business – Open for additional items not listed in the agenda. 4

i. Changes to qualifications for emeritus status - Some concerns have been transmitted to the Provost’s office and FSEC is waiting for a reply. ii. Brightspace purge - Faculty are complaining about the loss of resources but FSEC members agreed the 5-year horizon is more than reasonable and faculty members have the option of archiving materials themselves. It is not expected that the university will have Brightspace ‘forever’ and FSEC members queried if there is a plan in place for archiving or recovering materials after Brightspace is offboarded. Pres. Williams will assign the CTI the task of gleaning more information. iii. multiple paid resources for communications (CTI issue) - Tabled to next week’s meeting. 8. Closing Remarks – Recap of decisions made, action items, and plans for the next meeting. A question was asked about the recent Snow Day, wherein faculty were prevented from offering any remote synchronous options. Pres. Adjournment - The meeting adjourned at 2:34 pm. 5

Constitution, By-Laws and University Manual Committee Report # 2020-2021-2 to the Faculty Senate Faculty Senate Meeting February 18, 2021 Proposal to Change Faculty Senate Committee Structure The following recommended changes update the University Manual language passed by the Faculty Senate referring to the recently revised Faculty Senate committee structure (FS Bill # 20-21-14).
Recommended Changes: Motion: accept changes to the University Manual on committee structure language changes in 5.78.12, 5.84.13, 8.20.14, 8.20.17, 8.20.30, 8.70.10, 8.70.12, 8.70.13, 8.70.20, 8.70.61, 8.70.72, 8.81.50, 8.81.80 Changes: 5.78.12 Membership.
The committee shall comprise the Director of the Office for the Advancement of Teaching and Learning who shall serve as Chair, and the Assistant Director of Online Learning and the Director of Media & Technology Services by virtue of their positions.
The Provost shall appoint a designee from the Office of the Provost, and a dean of a degree-granting college.
The Faculty Senate shall appoint six faculty members to staggered three-year terms.

A graduate student and an undergraduate student, appointed respectively by the Graduate Student Association and the Student Senate, shall also serve on the committee.
The faculty appointees shall represent the University Libraries, the Curriculum and Standards Committee, the General Education Committee Subcommittee, and the Graduate Council and may represent more than one of these constituencies.
Faculty appointees may succeed themselves once. #12-13–1 #15-16-15D #16-17-21, #17-18-23 5.84.13 The membership shall include faculty members appointed by the Faculty Senate: two from Arts & Sciences, one from each of the other degree-granting colleges and one from the University Libraries, one faculty representative of each of the following committees: the Curriculum and Standards Committee, the General Education Committee Subcommittee, the Teaching, Advising, and Assessment Committee, and the Graduate Council.
Faculty representatives should be individuals involved in assessment in their departments/colleges.
All faculty appointments shall be for three-year staggered terms.

In addition, administrative members shall include the Vice Provost for Faculty Affairs; the Dean of University College for Academic Success or the dean’s designee; the dean of a degree-granting college; one designee of the Vice

President for Student Affairs; one representative of the Office of Institutional Research; the Director of the Office for the Advancement of Teaching and Learning or designee; and the Assistant Director of the Office of Student Learning, Outcomes Assessment, and Accreditation.
A graduate student and an undergraduate student, appointed respectively by the Graduate Student Association and the Student Senate, and a student representing the Alan Shawn Feinstein College of Education and Professional Studies, shall also serve on the committee.
A faculty member appointed by the Faculty Senate in consultation with the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs shall chair the committee. #06-07–25, #07-08–40 #14-15–31 #15-16-15D #16-17-21, #17-18-23 8.20.14 Any course that assesses two (2) of the General Education Student Learning Outcomes may be submitted to the Curriculum and Standards General Education Committee for approval to fulfill General Education requirements, regardless of that course’s place in a major or prerequisites.

No college, department, major, minor, or other program or course of study may require a student to choose a specific course to satisfy the General Education requirements, although courses that fulfill requirements or prerequisites for majors which also happen to satisfy General Education requirements can be recommended through advising.
Of the courses taken to complete General Education requirements, only up to 12 credits may share the same disciplinary code.
An exception to the limit is allowed for the HPR (Honors Program topic) course code.
Only courses that fulfill the D1 Student Learning Outcome, Integrate and Apply, may be graded using S/U.

Of D1 courses graded S/U, a student may apply only up to 6 credits to the total 40 credits needed to complete the General Education requirements. #13-14-21, #15-16-13 #16-17-26B, #17-18-23 8.20.17 The General Education Committee Subcommittee shall, through the using course review standards calibrated to those in use by the Curriculum and Standards Committee, make recommendations to the Faculty Senate regarding implementation and administration of General Education and shall report periodically its evaluation of the General Education Program, including a review of the appropriateness of courses for General Education. #13-14-21, #15-16-13, #17-18-23 8.20.30 Director of General Education.
A Director of General Education, selected from the University faculty, shall coordinate and advocate for the General Education Program.
The Director shall, in concert with the General Education Committee Subcommittee, be responsible for the overall management of the General Education Program.
The Director shall report to the President of the Faculty Senate, keeping the Faculty Senate Executive Committee informed of current issues as requested.
Questions of jurisdiction regarding joint responsibility for the General Education

Program shall be referred to the Faculty Senate.
The Director shall be released from one half of his/her normal duties and shall be compensated for work done during summers.
Normal duties shall include, but not be restricted to, teaching, assigned research, advisement, committee work and thesis direction. #16-17-31, #17-18-23 8.70.10 Preparation.
A six-year calendar for fall, winter, and spring semesters shall be maintained.
In accordance with sections 8.70.20-8.70.61, the Office of Enrollment Services each fall shall prepare a new sixth-year calendar and submit it to the Academic Calendar Committee Subcommittee by the end of October.
The Committee Subcommittee shall review the calendar and present it to the Curriculum and Standards Committee on time so that the calendar can be presented to the Faculty Senate by December 1. #01-02-27, #02-03–32, #12-13-21, #16-17-23, #17-18-23, #18-19-34 8.70.12 Unless acting in response to the declaration by the Senate Executive Committee of an emergency situation as stated in By-Laws 4.28, the Academic Calendar Committee Subcommittee, adjustments to a proposed calendar may not be made on the floor of the Senate.

Instead, a proposed calendar, along with instructions about possible revisions, must be referred back to the Academic Calendar Committee, which Subcommittee.
The Curriculum and Standards Committee shall resubmit the calendar at the next Senate meeting. #01-02-27, #16-17-23, #17-18-23 8.70.13 Recommendations regarding rescheduling class days missed within an academic year as the result of natural calamity, work stoppage, etc. shall be the responsibility of the Academic Calendar Committee Subcommittee, whose proposal shall be subject to the approval of the Curriculum and Standards Committee and subsequent approval by the Faculty Senate or, under circumstances requiring expeditious implementation, subject to the approval of the Faculty Senate Executive Committee only after a public hearing on the action scheduled with at least a 48 hour notice. #05-06–1 #14-15-32, #16- 17-23, #17-18-23 8.70.20 The Academic Year.
The beginning and ending dates of each semester shall be the same for all colleges and schools of the University.

Exceptions may be granted to the Alan Shawn Feinstein College of Education and Professional Studies and to fully-online accelerated programs (which will run on the fully-online accelerated calendar).
Requests for exceptions shall be received by the Curriculum and Standards Committee on time such that they can be transmitted to the Academic Calendar Committee Subcommittee no later than October 1 of the preceding academic year. #14-15–08, #16-17-23, #17-18-23

8.70.61 A six-year calendar for the Summer Session shall be maintained.
The Office of Enrollment Services, in consultation with the Assistant Director of Summer Session and Winter J-Term, each fall shall prepare a new sixth-year calendar and submit it to the Academic Calendar Committee Subcommittee by the end of October.
The Committee Subcommittee shall review the calendar and present it to the Curriculum and Standards Committee on time so that the calendar can be presented to the Faculty Senate by December 1. #01-02-27 #16-17-16, #16-17-23, #17-18-23, #18-19-34 8.70.72 The two-year calendar for the fully-online accelerated program shall be developed by the Office of Online Education, in consultation with the Office of Enrollment Services, and submitted to the Academic Calendar Committee Subcommittee by March 1 of the year preceding the one during which the calendar is to become effective.

The Academic Calendar Committee Subcommittee shall review the calendar for the fully-online accelerated program and present it to the Curriculum and Standards Committee on time so that it can be presented to the Faculty Senate for approval by April 1 of the year preceding the one during which the calendar is to become effective. #14-15–08, #16-17-23, #17-18-23, #18-19-34 8.81.50 Scheduling Courses.
Courses submitted to the Office of Enrollment Services for scheduling shall be certified by the department chairperson via the academic dean as being permanently approved or authorized temporary courses.
A new course or course change proposal form must be processed through the college curriculum committee, Curriculum and Standards Committee or General Education Committee where appropriate, and/or Graduate Council, and approved by the Faculty Senate before being scheduled. #17-18-23 8.81.80 Course Jurisdiction.
The content, textbook, over-all conduct and method of presentation of single section courses shall be the responsibility of the instructor.
The administration of multi-section courses shall be determined by departments.

Modifications that significantly change a course (e.g. lecture to online offering, lecture and lab to lecture) require approval through the proper curricular channels (e.g. college curriculum committees) to the Curriculum and Standards Committee or General Education Committee when appropriate, and/or the Graduate Council, and the Faculty Senate. #06-07-33, #17-18-23

Constitution, By-Laws and University Manual Committee Report # 2020-2021-3 to the Faculty Senate Faculty Senate Meeting February 18, 2021 Proposal to Revise Definition of General Faculty Definition of General Faculty The Faculty Senate Executive Committee and the Constitution, By-laws and University Manual Committee recommend that the following changes be made to the UM in order to clarify the definition of General Faculty. This recommended change makes it clear that all faculty are members of the General Faculty and are welcome and have the right to participate in General Faculty meetings and the right to vote on matters requiring a vote of the General Faculty such as conferral of degrees and changes to the Constitution. Motion: accept recommended change to 4.11.10; 4.11.10 Membership in the University Faculty, also referred to as the General Faculty, shall be based on appointment by the President and on direct participation in or supervision of any of the following activities: teaching, librarianship, and research and creative activities, within the University. General Faculty includes those appointed to full-time tenure-track and non tenure-track positions. The General Faculty shall consist of tenure-track professors, associate professors, assistant professors, instructors (see 7.10.10); t The President, the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs, the Vice President for Research and Economic Development, the Vice Provost(s), and the academic dean and associate dean(s) of each college or school and of the library are also part of the General Faculty. #15-16-29

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND FACULTY SENATE October 15, 2020 Faculty Senate Curriculum and Standards Committee Report 2020-2021-1 At the October 1, 2020 meeting of the Curriculum and Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate. SECTION II Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by the Faculty Senate NEW PROGRAMS: COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES: New Interdisciplinary Minor in Social Justice and Civic Responsibilities: We propose an undergraduate interdisciplinary minor in Social Justice & Civic Responsibilities. The United Nations defines social justice in terms of human rights and personal dignity for everyone. Other sources include access and equality. Borrowing from these descriptions, we define social justice broadly as the value of human life, equal access to social capital, personal dignity, and the implementation of human rights for ALL. US Citizenship and Immigration Services identifies core civic responsibilities that include staying informed about issues affecting your community and participating in them. More importantly they add respecting the rights, beliefs, and opinions of others, and participating in the democratic process. We adopt these descriptions of civic responsibilities for the minor.

Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages) We propose an undergraduate interdisciplinary minor in Social Justice & Civic Responsibilities.
The United Nations defines social justice in terms of human rights and personal dignity for everyone.
Other sources include access and equality.
Borrowing from these descriptions, we define social justice broadly as the value of human life, equal access to social capital, personal dignity, and the implementation of human rights for ALL.
US Citizenship and Immigration Services identifies core civic responsibilities that include staying informed about issues affecting your community and participating in them.
More importantly they add respecting the rights, beliefs, and opinions of others, and participating in the democratic process.
We adopt these descriptions of civic responsibilities for the minor.
Course options for the minor represent an array of multidisciplinary and interdisciplinary approaches to social justice topics.
